claim: Red blood cells (RBCs) experience significant mechanical forces while recirculating.
source: Red blood cells (RBCs) experience significant mechanical forces while recirculating, but the consequences of these forces are not fully understood.
evidence: This is stated as established context in the abstract without specific supporting data in this manuscript, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in mechanically activated Piezo1 cation channels are associated with the dehydrating RBC disease xerocytosis.
source: Recent work has shown that gain-of-function mutations in mechanically activated Piezo1 cation channels are associated with the dehydrating RBC disease xerocytosis, implicating a role of mechanotransduction in RBC volume regulation.
evidence: This claim references 'recent work' which is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: RBCs exhibit robust calcium entry in response to mechanical stretch.
source: In this study, we show that RBCs exhibit robust calcium entry in response to mechanical stretch and that this entry is dependent on Piezo1 expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Calcium entry in RBCs in response to mechanical stretch is dependent on Piezo1 expression.
source: In this study, we show that RBCs exhibit robust calcium entry in response to mechanical stretch and that this entry is dependent on Piezo1 expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing WT and Piezo1-deficient RBCs in Figure 2D.

claim: RBCs from blood-cell-specific Piezo1 conditional knockout mice are overhydrated.
source: Furthermore, RBCs from blood-cell-specific Piezo1 conditional knockout mice are overhydrated and exhibit increased fragility both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by hematological data in Table 1 and osmotic fragility data in Figure 1C.

claim: RBCs from blood-cell-specific Piezo1 conditional knockout mice exhibit increased fragility both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Furthermore, RBCs from blood-cell-specific Piezo1 conditional knockout mice are overhydrated and exhibit increased fragility both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: In vitro fragility is shown in Figure 1C, and in vivo fragility is indicated by reduced plasma haptoglobin in Figure 1E.

claim: Yoda1, a chemical activator of Piezo1, causes calcium influx in RBCs.
source: Finally, we show that Yoda1, a chemical activator of Piezo1, causes calcium influx and subsequent dehydration of RBCs via downstream activation of the KCa3.1 Gardos channel, directly implicating Piezo1 signaling in RBC volume control.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A showing increased Fluo-4 fluorescence.

claim: Yoda1 causes subsequent dehydration of RBCs via downstream activation of the KCa3.1 Gardos channel.
source: Finally, we show that Yoda1, a chemical activator of Piezo1, causes calcium influx and subsequent dehydration of RBCs via downstream activation of the KCa3.1 Gardos channel, directly implicating Piezo1 signaling in RBC volume control.
evidence: This is supported by osmotic fragility experiments in Figure 3C showing that TRAM-34 (KCa3.1 antagonist) prevents Yoda1-induced dehydration.

claim: Mechanically activated Piezo1 plays an essential role in RBC volume homeostasis.
source: Therefore, mechanically activated Piezo1 plays an essential role in RBC volume homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mammalian red blood cells lack a nucleus and many organelles.
source: Mammalian red blood cells (RBCs) are rather unique in that they lack a nucleus and many organelles and that they traverse the circulatory system several hundred thousand times in their life cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RBC biology.

claim: RBCs traverse the circulatory system several hundred thousand times in their life cycle.
source: Mammalian red blood cells (RBCs) are rather unique in that they lack a nucleus and many organelles and that they traverse the circulatory system several hundred thousand times in their life cycle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RBC circulation.

claim: RBCs experience mechanical forces that influence their deformability.
source: RBCs experience significant mechanical forces while recirculating that influence their physiology in many ways, including changes in deformability (Chien, 1987), ATP release (Sprague et al., 2001), NO release (Yalcin et al., 2008), and Ca2+ influx (Larsen et al., 1981; Dyrda and et al., 2010), the latter of which can influence RBC volume.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chien, 1987.

claim: Mechanical forces on RBCs influence ATP release.
source: RBCs experience significant mechanical forces while recirculating that influence their physiology in many ways, including changes in deformability (Chien, 1987), ATP release (Sprague et al., 2001), NO release (Yalcin et al., 2008), and Ca2+ influx (Larsen et al., 1981; Dyrda and et al., 2010), the latter of which can influence RBC volume.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sprague et al., 2001.

claim: Mechanical forces on RBCs influence NO release.
source: RBCs experience significant mechanical forces while recirculating that influence their physiology in many ways, including changes in deformability (Chien, 1987), ATP release (Sprague et al., 2001), NO release (Yalcin et al., 2008), and Ca2+ influx (Larsen et al., 1981; Dyrda and et al., 2010), the latter of which can influence RBC volume.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yalcin et al., 2008.

claim: Mechanical forces on RBCs influence Ca2+ influx.
source: RBCs experience significant mechanical forces while recirculating that influence their physiology in many ways, including changes in deformability (Chien, 1987), ATP release (Sprague et al., 2001), NO release (Yalcin et al., 2008), and Ca2+ influx (Larsen et al., 1981; Dyrda and et al., 2010), the latter of which can influence RBC volume.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Larsen et al., 1981 and Dyrda and et al., 2010.

claim: Ca2+ influx can influence RBC volume.
source: RBCs experience significant mechanical forces while recirculating that influence their physiology in many ways, including changes in deformability (Chien, 1987), ATP release (Sprague et al., 2001), NO release (Yalcin et al., 2008), and Ca2+ influx (Larsen et al., 1981; Dyrda and et al., 2010), the latter of which can influence RBC volume.
evidence: This is stated based on prior literature and is a key premise for the study.

claim: Changes in RBC volume can affect their membrane integrity.
source: Changes in RBC volume can affect their membrane integrity and ability to travel through capillaries with diameters smaller than the RBCs themselves.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of RBC physiology.

claim: Changes in RBC volume can affect their ability to travel through capillaries with diameters smaller than the RBCs themselves.
source: Changes in RBC volume can affect their membrane integrity and ability to travel through capillaries with diameters smaller than the RBCs themselves.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of RBC physiology and deformability.

claim: Several pathologies result from either overhydration or dehydration of RBCs.
source: The critical importance of RBC volume regulation is demonstrated by several pathologies resulting from either overhydration or dehydration of RBCs (Gallagher, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gallagher, 2013.

claim: Piezo1 and Piezo2 are a conserved family of mechanosensitive non-selective cation channels.
source: Recent studies have identified a conserved family of mechanosensitive non-selective cation channels, Piezo1 and Piezo2 (Coste et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coste et al., 2010, 2012.

claim: Piezo1 responds to a wide array of mechanical forces, including poking, stretching, and shear stress.
source: Piezo1 responds to a wide array of mechanical forces, including poking, stretching, and shear stress, and is essential for proper vascular development in mice (Nilius and Honore, 2012; Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nilius and Honore, 2012; Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014.

claim: Piezo1 is essential for proper vascular development in mice.
source: Piezo1 responds to a wide array of mechanical forces, including poking, stretching, and shear stress, and is essential for proper vascular development in mice (Nilius and Honore, 2012; Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nilius and Honore, 2012; Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014.

claim: Many gain-of-function mutations in Piezo1 have been identified in patients with xerocytosis (dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis).
source: The potential role of Piezo1 in RBC physiology is most clearly demonstrated by many gain-of-function mutations in Piezo1 that have been identified in patients with the RBC disease xerocytosis, also called dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis (DHS) (Zarychanski et al., 2012; Albuisson et al., 2013; Andolfo et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zarychanski et al., 2012; Albuisson et al., 2013; Andolfo et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013.

claim: Whole body treatment of zebrafish with Piezo1 morpholino affects RBC volume homeostasis.
source: In addition, whole body treatment of zebrafish with Piezo1 morpholino affects RBC volume homeostasis (Faucherre et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Faucherre et al., 2014.

claim: The Piezo1 locus has been implicated in a genome-wide association screen for affecting the RBC mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) in humans.
source: Finally, the Piezo1 locus has also been implicated in a genome-wide association screen for affecting the RBC mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) in humans (van der Harst et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van der Harst et al., 2012.

claim: Peripheral blood RBCs from Piezo1P1-tdTomato mice exhibited increased tdTomato fluorescence compared to those from Piezo1+/+ mice.
source: Both peripheral blood RBCs (Figure 1A) and developing bone marrow pro-RBCs (Figure 1B) from Piezo1P1-tdTomato mice exhibited increased tdTomato fluorescence by flow cytometry compared to those from Piezo1+/+ mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Developing bone marrow pro-RBCs from Piezo1P1-tdTomato mice exhibited increased tdTomato fluorescence compared to those from Piezo1+/+ mice.
source: Both peripheral blood RBCs (Figure 1A) and developing bone marrow pro-RBCs (Figure 1B) from Piezo1P1-tdTomato mice exhibited increased tdTomato fluorescence by flow cytometry compared to those from Piezo1+/+ mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Peripheral RBCs from Piezo1P1-tdTomato mice had clear expression of a ∼320 kDa Piezo1-tdTomato fusion protein.
source: Peripheral RBCs from Piezo1P1-tdTomato mice had clear expression of a ∼320 kDa Piezo1-tdTomato fusion protein by Western blot (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mice deficient in Piezo1 die in utero.
source: Mice deficient in Piezo1 die in utero, so we deleted Piezo1 specifically in the hematopoietic system.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, likely from prior literature.

claim: Vav1-iCre mice express Cre recombinase early in hematopoiesis.
source: We bred Vav1-iCre mice, which express Cre recombinase early in hematopoiesis (Shimshek et al., 2002), to mice where exons 20–23 of Piezo1 are flanked by loxP sites (P1f), thus generating viable, fertile Vav1-iCre P1f/f (Vav1-P1cKO) mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shimshek et al., 2002.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO mice are viable and fertile.
source: We bred Vav1-iCre mice, which express Cre recombinase early in hematopoiesis (Shimshek et al., 2002), to mice where exons 20–23 of Piezo1 are flanked by loxP sites (P1f), thus generating viable, fertile Vav1-iCre P1f/f (Vav1-P1cKO) mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the generation of the mouse model.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO lymphocytes exhibited >95% deletion of piezo1 transcript.
source: Vav1-P1cKO lymphocytes exhibited >95% deletion of piezo1 transcript, demonstrating efficient Cre-mediated excision (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO mice had elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV) compared to WT mice.
source: Notably, compared to WT mice, Vav1-P1cKO mice had elevated (% of WT ± SEM) mean corpuscular volume (MCV, 109.51 ± 1.51) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH, 103.14 ± 0.48) and reduced mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC, 94.37 ± 1.08), suggesting that Piezo1-deficient RBCs were overhydrated.
evidence: This is supported by hematological data presented in Table 1.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO mice had elevated mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) compared to WT mice.
source: Notably, compared to WT mice, Vav1-P1cKO mice had elevated (% of WT ± SEM) mean corpuscular volume (MCV, 109.51 ± 1.51) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH, 103.14 ± 0.48) and reduced mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC, 94.37 ± 1.08), suggesting that Piezo1-deficient RBCs were overhydrated.
evidence: This is supported by hematological data presented in Table 1.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO mice had reduced mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) compared to WT mice.
source: Notably, compared to WT mice, Vav1-P1cKO mice had elevated (% of WT ± SEM) mean corpuscular volume (MCV, 109.51 ± 1.51) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH, 103.14 ± 0.48) and reduced mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC, 94.37 ± 1.08), suggesting that Piezo1-deficient RBCs were overhydrated.
evidence: This is supported by hematological data presented in Table 1.

claim: Piezo1-deficient RBCs were overhydrated.
source: Notably, compared to WT mice, Vav1-P1cKO mice had elevated (% of WT ± SEM) mean corpuscular volume (MCV, 109.51 ± 1.51) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH, 103.14 ± 0.48) and reduced mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC, 94.37 ± 1.08), suggesting that Piezo1-deficient RBCs were overhydrated.
evidence: This is inferred from the hematological indices and confirmed by osmotic fragility and flow cytometry data.

claim: Overhydrated RBCs exhibit increased osmotic fragility.
source: Overhydrated RBCs exhibit increased osmotic fragility and increased size as measured by forward scatter using flow cytometry.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RBC physiology.

claim: Overhydrated RBCs exhibit increased size as measured by forward scatter using flow cytometry.
source: Overhydrated RBCs exhibit increased osmotic fragility and increased size as measured by forward scatter using flow cytometry.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RBC physiology and flow cytometry measurements.

claim: Blood from Vav1-P1cKO mice exhibited increased osmotic fragility.
source: Blood from Vav1-P1cKO mice exhibited both of these characteristics (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), demonstrating that Piezo1-deficient RBCs are overhydrated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by osmotic fragility data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Blood from Vav1-P1cKO mice exhibited increased RBC size.
source: Blood from Vav1-P1cKO mice exhibited both of these characteristics (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), demonstrating that Piezo1-deficient RBCs are overhydrated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by forward scatter data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO RBCs had relatively normal discoid morphology.
source: While Vav1-P1cKO RBCs were overhydrated, scanning electron microscopy of WT and Vav1-P1cKO RBCs revealed that Vav1-P1cKO RBCs had relatively normal discoid morphology, unlike more severe overhydration pathologies such as spherocytosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scanning electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Piezo1 expression on RBCs is a negative regulator of RBC volume.
source: Regardless, these results suggest that Piezo1 expression on RBCs is a negative regulator of RBC volume.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Piezo1-deficient RBCs are overhydrated.

claim: Spleens from Vav1-P1cKO mice appeared visibly darker and redder following H&E staining.
source: Although they appeared visibly darker and redder following H&E staining, spleens from Vav1-P1cKO mice exhibited normal formation of both red and white pulp without an evident expansion of red pulp or increased iron deposition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is an observation from histological analysis.

claim: Spleens from Vav1-P1cKO mice exhibited normal formation of both red and white pulp.
source: Although they appeared visibly darker and redder following H&E staining, spleens from Vav1-P1cKO mice exhibited normal formation of both red and white pulp without an evident expansion of red pulp or increased iron deposition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO spleens had an increased number of fully mature Ter119+ CD71− RBCs.
source: However, flow cytometric analysis of splenic RBC subpopulations revealed an increased number of fully mature Ter119+ CD71− RBCs, but not immature Ter119+ CD71+ RBCs (Figure 1D), suggesting that the darker splenic color is due in part to retention of overhydrated circulating mature RBCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO spleens did not have an increased number of immature Ter119+ CD71+ RBCs.
source: However, flow cytometric analysis of splenic RBC subpopulations revealed an increased number of fully mature Ter119+ CD71− RBCs, but not immature Ter119+ CD71+ RBCs (Figure 1D), suggesting that the darker splenic color is due in part to retention of overhydrated circulating mature RBCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The darker splenic color in Vav1-P1cKO mice is due in part to retention of overhydrated circulating mature RBCs.
source: However, flow cytometric analysis of splenic RBC subpopulations revealed an increased number of fully mature Ter119+ CD71− RBCs, but not immature Ter119+ CD71+ RBCs (Figure 1D), suggesting that the darker splenic color is due in part to retention of overhydrated circulating mature RBCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased number of mature RBCs in the spleen.

claim: Immature splenic RBCs had similar forward scatter in WT and Vav1-P1cKO mice.
source: Consistent with this, immature splenic RBCs had similar forward scatter in WT and Vav1-P1cKO mice, indicating that they were of similar size, while fully mature RBCs in Vav1-P1cKO exhibited increased forward scatter indicative of increased size (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Fully mature RBCs in Vav1-P1cKO exhibited increased forward scatter indicative of increased size.
source: Consistent with this, immature splenic RBCs had similar forward scatter in WT and Vav1-P1cKO mice, indicating that they were of similar size, while fully mature RBCs in Vav1-P1cKO exhibited increased forward scatter indicative of increased size (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO mice exhibited significantly lower plasma haptoglobin concentrations.
source: We also found that Vav1-P1cKO mice exhibited significantly lower plasma haptoglobin concentrations, indicative of intravascular hemolysis in vivo (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Lower plasma haptoglobin concentrations are indicative of intravascular hemolysis in vivo.
source: We also found that Vav1-P1cKO mice exhibited significantly lower plasma haptoglobin concentrations, indicative of intravascular hemolysis in vivo (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about haptoglobin as a marker of hemolysis.

claim: Piezo1-deficient RBCs have increased fragility.
source: Thus, Piezo1-deficient RBCs have increased fragility and are aberrantly retained within the spleen, suggesting that Piezo1 helps maintain RBC integrity and normal recirculation.
evidence: This is concluded from the osmotic fragility and haptoglobin data.

claim: Piezo1-deficient RBCs are aberrantly retained within the spleen.
source: Thus, Piezo1-deficient RBCs have increased fragility and are aberrantly retained within the spleen, suggesting that Piezo1 helps maintain RBC integrity and normal recirculation.
evidence: This is concluded from the increased number of mature RBCs in the spleen.

claim: Piezo1 helps maintain RBC integrity and normal recirculation.
source: Thus, Piezo1-deficient RBCs have increased fragility and are aberrantly retained within the spleen, suggesting that Piezo1 helps maintain RBC integrity and normal recirculation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed phenotypes of Piezo1-deficient RBCs.

claim: Piezo1 is a mechanically activated, calcium-permeable non-selective cation channel.
source: Piezo1 is a mechanically activated, calcium-permeable non-selective cation channel.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Piezo1 from prior literature.

claim: Application of negative pressure induced a rapid rise in intracellular Ca2+ levels in Fluo-4-loaded WT RBCs with a threshold of ∼ −5 mmHg.
source: Application of negative pressure induced a rapid rise in intracellular Ca2+ levels in Fluo-4-loaded WT RBCs with a threshold of ∼ −5 mmHg and a P50 of −9.72 ± 0.51 mmHg (Figure 2B,C and Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Application of negative pressure induced a rapid rise in intracellular Ca2+ levels in Fluo-4-loaded WT RBCs with a P50 of −9.72 ± 0.51 mmHg.
source: Application of negative pressure induced a rapid rise in intracellular Ca2+ levels in Fluo-4-loaded WT RBCs with a threshold of ∼ −5 mmHg and a P50 of −9.72 ± 0.51 mmHg (Figure 2B,C and Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Following removal of a half-maximal −10 mmHg stimulus, Ca2+ levels declined to baseline with an average t1/2 of 21 ± 1.8 s.
source: Following removal of a half-maximal −10 mmHg stimulus, Ca2+ levels declined to baseline with an average t1/2 of 21 ± 1.8 s.
evidence: This is calculated from calcium imaging data.

claim: The increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration in RBCs in response to mechanical stretch is a result of influx rather than receptor-mediated store release.
source: This increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration must be a result of influx rather than receptor-mediated store release as RBCs do not possess intracellular stores.
evidence: This is inferred from the known biology of RBCs lacking intracellular calcium stores.

claim: RBCs do not possess intracellular calcium stores.
source: This increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration must be a result of influx rather than receptor-mediated store release as RBCs do not possess intracellular stores.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RBC biology.

claim: Ca2+ influx was not detectable in any Vav1-P1cKO RBCs, even at pressures up to −35 mmHg.
source: We found that Ca2+ influx was not detectable in any Vav1-P1cKO RBCs, even at pressures up to −35 mmHg (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: RBCs can respond to mechanical force by allowing Ca2+ to enter the cell.
source: These results demonstrate that RBCs can respond to mechanical force by allowing Ca2+ to enter the cell and that this Ca2+ influx is dependent on Piezo1.
evidence: This is concluded from the calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Mechanically-induced Ca2+ influx in RBCs is dependent on Piezo1.
source: These results demonstrate that RBCs can respond to mechanical force by allowing Ca2+ to enter the cell and that this Ca2+ influx is dependent on Piezo1.
evidence: This is concluded from the absence of Ca2+ influx in Piezo1-deficient RBCs.

claim: RBCs from one strain of mice lacking KCa3.1 exhibit increased size and osmotic fragility similar to what is seen in Vav1-P1cKO mice.
source: In fact, RBCs from one strain of mice lacking KCa3.1 exhibit increased size and osmotic fragility similar to what is seen in Vav1-P1cKO mice (Grgic et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grgic et al., 2009.

claim: Yoda1 caused robust increases in fluorescence of WT, but not in Vav1-P1cKO RBCs.
source: Yoda1 caused robust increases in fluorescence of WT, but not in Vav1-P1cKO RBCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both WT and Vav1-P1cKO RBCs exhibited similar Ca2+ influx in response to the Ca2+ ionophore A23187.
source: In contrast, both WT and Vav1-P1cKO RBCs exhibited similar Ca2+ influx in response to the Ca2+ ionophore A23187 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A rise in intracellular Ca2+ in response to Yoda1 would be expected to activate KCa3.1.
source: A rise in intracellular Ca2+ in response to Yoda1 would be expected to activate KCa3.1, also known as the Gardos channel, which can mediate K+ efflux, H2O efflux, and RBC dehydration (Maher and Kuchel, 2003).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about KCa3.1 function, supported by citation to Maher and Kuchel, 2003.

claim: KCa3.1 can mediate K+ efflux, H2O efflux, and RBC dehydration.
source: A rise in intracellular Ca2+ in response to Yoda1 would be expected to activate KCa3.1, also known as the Gardos channel, which can mediate K+ efflux, H2O efflux, and RBC dehydration (Maher and Kuchel, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maher and Kuchel, 2003.

claim: Treatment of WT RBCs with 15 μM Yoda1 led to a rapid change in their shape, progressing from discocytes to echinocytes to spherocytes.
source: Treatment of WT RBCs, but not Vav1-P1cKO RBCs, with 15 μM Yoda1 led to a rapid change in their shape, progressing from discocytes to echinocytes to spherocytes, similar to what has been demonstrated for treatment with A23187 (Steffen et al., 2011) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by brightfield imaging shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment of Vav1-P1cKO RBCs with 15 μM Yoda1 did not lead to a change in their shape.
source: Treatment of WT RBCs, but not Vav1-P1cKO RBCs, with 15 μM Yoda1 led to a rapid change in their shape, progressing from discocytes to echinocytes to spherocytes, similar to what has been demonstrated for treatment with A23187 (Steffen et al., 2011) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by brightfield imaging shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment with A23187 causes RBC shape changes similar to Yoda1.
source: Treatment of WT RBCs, but not Vav1-P1cKO RBCs, with 15 μM Yoda1 led to a rapid change in their shape, progressing from discocytes to echinocytes to spherocytes, similar to what has been demonstrated for treatment with A23187 (Steffen et al., 2011) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steffen et al., 2011.

claim: Incubation of WT blood for 30 min with 5 μM Yoda1 caused a marked reduction in RBC osmotic fragility.
source: Incubation of WT, but not Vav1-P1cKO blood, for 30 min with 5 μM Yoda1 caused a marked reduction in RBC osmotic fragility that was prevented by a 10-min pretreatment with 2 μM TRAM-34 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by osmotic fragility data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Incubation of Vav1-P1cKO blood for 30 min with 5 μM Yoda1 did not cause a reduction in RBC osmotic fragility.
source: Incubation of WT, but not Vav1-P1cKO blood, for 30 min with 5 μM Yoda1 caused a marked reduction in RBC osmotic fragility that was prevented by a 10-min pretreatment with 2 μM TRAM-34 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by osmotic fragility data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Yoda1-induced reduction in RBC osmotic fragility was prevented by pretreatment with TRAM-34.
source: Incubation of WT, but not Vav1-P1cKO blood, for 30 min with 5 μM Yoda1 caused a marked reduction in RBC osmotic fragility that was prevented by a 10-min pretreatment with 2 μM TRAM-34 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by osmotic fragility data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both WT and Vav1-P1cKO RBCs exhibited reduced osmotic fragility when treated for 30 min with 1 μM A23187.
source: Both WT and Vav1-P1cKO RBCs exhibited reduced osmotic fragility when treated for 30 min with 1 μM A23187, demonstrating normal functionality of KCa3.1 in Vav1-P1cKO RBCs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by osmotic fragility data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: KCa3.1 has normal functionality in Vav1-P1cKO RBCs.
source: Both WT and Vav1-P1cKO RBCs exhibited reduced osmotic fragility when treated for 30 min with 1 μM A23187, demonstrating normal functionality of KCa3.1 in Vav1-P1cKO RBCs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar response to A23187 in both genotypes.

claim: The lack of any Ca2+ influx, shape changes, or changes in osmotic fragility of Vav1-P1cKO RBCs in response to Yoda1 demonstrates the specificity of Yoda1 on Piezo1.
source: The lack of any Ca2+ influx, shape changes, or changes in osmotic fragility of Vav1-P1cKO RBCs in response to Yoda1 further demonstrates the specificity of Yoda1 on Piezo1.
evidence: This is inferred from the complete absence of Yoda1 effects in Piezo1-deficient RBCs.

claim: TRAM-34 did not block Piezo1 in HEK293T cells transfected with Piezo1.
source: Importantly, TRAM-34 did not block Piezo1 HEK293T cells transfected with Piezo1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activation of Piezo1 on RBCs leads to calcium influx, potassium efflux through KCa3.1 that is accompanied by water loss, resulting in RBC dehydration.
source: These data as a whole suggest a model shown in Figure 3E whereby activation of Piezo1 on RBCs leads to calcium influx, potassium efflux through KCa3.1 that is accompanied by water loss, resulting in RBC dehydration.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the collective experimental findings.

claim: The ability of RBCs to reduce their volume in response to mechanical forces could improve their ability to traverse through small-diameter capillaries and splenic sinusoids.
source: The ability of RBCs to reduce their volume in response to mechanical forces could improve their ability to traverse through small-diameter capillaries and splenic sinusoids.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Reduction in RBC volume could aid in oxygen/CO2 exchange in the periphery by concentrating hemoglobin within RBCs.
source: Additionally, it is possible that this reduction in volume could aid in oxygen/CO2 exchange in the periphery by concentrating hemoglobin within RBCs, which may promote release of oxygen from hemoglobin; in fact, mechanical stimulation of RBCs via optical tweezers has been shown to cause such a release of oxygen (Rao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to Rao et al., 2009.

claim: Mechanical stimulation of RBCs via optical tweezers has been shown to cause release of oxygen.
source: Additionally, it is possible that this reduction in volume could aid in oxygen/CO2 exchange in the periphery by concentrating hemoglobin within RBCs, which may promote release of oxygen from hemoglobin; in fact, mechanical stimulation of RBCs via optical tweezers has been shown to cause such a release of oxygen (Rao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rao et al., 2009.

claim: Genetic deletion of Piezo1 in blood cells leads to overhydrated, fragile RBCs.
source: We have demonstrated that genetic deletion of Piezo1 in blood cells leads to overhydrated, fragile RBCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the Vav1-P1cKO mouse experiments.

claim: Mechanical force can cause calcium influx into RBCs that is dependent on Piezo1 expression.
source: We have also shown that mechanical force can cause calcium influx into RBCs that is dependent on Piezo1 expression.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the mechanical stimulation experiments.

claim: Calcium influx through Piezo1 dehydrates RBCs via the actions of KCa3.1.
source: Finally, using the first identified selective small molecule activator of Piezo1, we have shown that calcium influx through Piezo1 dehydrates RBCs via the actions of KCa3.1.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the Yoda1 experiments.

claim: The dehydration seen in DHS patients is due to increased Piezo1-mediated calcium influx in response to mechanical forces in RBCs themselves.
source: These findings are consistent with the observation of dehydrated RBCs from DHS patients with gain-of-function Piezo1 mutations (Zarychanski et al., 2012; Albuisson et al., 2013; Andolfo et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013), further supporting that the dehydration seen in DHS patients is due to increased Piezo1-mediated calcium influx in response to mechanical forces in RBCs themselves.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of the findings with DHS patient observations.

claim: Piezo1 has been proposed to mediate a non-selective current observed in sickle cell disease (SCD) called PSickle.
source: Piezo1 has been proposed by many to mediate a non-selective current observed in sickle cell disease (SCD) called PSickle, which acts upstream of KCa3.1 to mediate RBC sickling (Lew et al., 1997; Ranney, 1997; Ma et al., 2012; Demolombe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lew et al., 1997; Ranney, 1997; Ma et al., 2012; Demolombe et al., 2013.

claim: PSickle acts upstream of KCa3.1 to mediate RBC sickling.
source: Piezo1 has been proposed by many to mediate a non-selective current observed in sickle cell disease (SCD) called PSickle, which acts upstream of KCa3.1 to mediate RBC sickling (Lew et al., 1997; Ranney, 1997; Ma et al., 2012; Demolombe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lew et al., 1997; Ranney, 1997; Ma et al., 2012; Demolombe et al., 2013.

claim: KCa3.1 inhibitors can improve many hematological indices of SCD patients.
source: While KCa3.1 inhibitors can improve many hematological indices of SCD patients, they have thus far been ineffective in preventing painful vasculo-occlusive crises (Ataga et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ataga et al., 2008.

claim: KCa3.1 inhibitors have been ineffective in preventing painful vasculo-occlusive crises in SCD patients.
source: While KCa3.1 inhibitors can improve many hematological indices of SCD patients, they have thus far been ineffective in preventing painful vasculo-occlusive crises (Ataga et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ataga et al., 2008.

claim: Inhibiting Piezo1 may modulate other pathways in addition to potentially blocking KCa3.1-dependent dehydration that may have therapeutic benefits in patients with SCD.
source: Inhibiting Piezo1 may modulate other pathways in addition to potentially blocking KCa3.1-dependent dehydration that may have therapeutic benefits in patients with SCD.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: Piezo1P1-tdTomato mice express a Piezo1-tdTomato fusion protein from the Piezo1 locus.
source: We first investigated whether Piezo1 is expressed on mouse RBCs using Piezo1P1-tdTomato mice that express a Piezo1-tdTomato fusion protein from the Piezo1 locus (Ranade et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ranade et al., 2014.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO mice do not have significant anemia.
source: Hematological analysis of blood from Vav1-P1cKO mice revealed significant changes in RBC physiology without significant anemia (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated based on hematological data in Table 1.

claim: Increased MCV can be observed in dehydrated RBCs in xerocytosis.
source: Since increased MCV can also be observed in the dehydrated RBCs in xerocytosis, we further tested whether Piezo1-deficient RBCs were actually overhydrated.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about xerocytosis.

claim: Yoda1 is a Piezo1-selective activator.
source: To directly test the effect that Piezo1 activation could have on RBC volume, we utilized the recently identified Piezo1-selective activator Yoda1 (Syeda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Syeda et al., 2015.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO mice had a reduced red blood cell count compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with statistical significance indicated.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO mice had elevated hematocrit (HCT) compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with statistical significance indicated.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO mice had elevated red cell distribution width (RDW) compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with statistical significance indicated.

claim: Vav1-P1cKO mice had similar hemoglobin content (HGB) compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 without statistical significance.
